title: Not All RFCs are Standards
summary: Explains that publication as an RFC does not make a document an Internet Standard. Many RFCs are informational, experimental, or historic, and only those that go through the standards process carry that status.

plainLanguage.summary: Being printed in a book does not make something a rule. Only some RFCs are rules, and this tells you that.

questions: what is the difference between an rfc and a standard
subtitle: Publishing a document as an RFC does not make it an Internet Standard.

tldr.problem: People confuse RFCs published as informational or experimental notes with real Internet standards, which can mislead vendors and customers.
tldr.mechanism: The memo points out that every RFC has a status, that standards also carry STD numbers, and that the IAB proposes to publicize standards status more, including an html version of STD-1.
tldr.outcome: The IAB keeps the single RFC series because publication is better than ignorance. The memo is Informational and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Standards Track levels
facts.value: Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, Internet Standard

today: RFC 1796 is an Informational memo and, according to its metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. Its explanation of RFC status and STD numbers is as the IAB gave it in April 1995.

sections.title: The Misconception
sections.content:
The RFC series is the official publication channel for Internet standards documents and other publications of the IESG, IAB and Internet community. About every six months in recent years, someone has questioned publishing both standards and informational documents as RFCs, on the argument that it confuses "real standards" with "mere publications".

The memo calls it a regrettably wide-spread misconception that publication as an RFC provides some level of recognition. It does not, or at least not any more than publication in a regular journal.
sections.plainLanguage: Some people think that if a paper is in the RFC collection, it must be an official rule. That is not true, just as not every journal article is a law.

sections.title: Status and STD Numbers
sections.content:
Each RFC has a status relative to the standardization process: Informational, Experimental, Standards Track (Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, Internet Standard), or Historic. The status is on the RFC's first page and in the periodic "Internet Official Protocols Standards" RFC (STD 1), but quotes and references often leave it out.

When a specification becomes an Internet Standard it gets the extra label "STD xxxx" but keeps its RFC number and its place in the series. STD numbers identify protocols, and RFC numbers identify documents, so the relationship is not one to one.

To publicize standards status, the IAB proposes to use STD numbers in cross references between standards track documents, and to add an html version of STD-1 using "web" hypertext technology.
sections.plainLanguage: Every RFC wears a name tag saying what kind it is. The official rules also get a second tag, STD, but they keep their old number.

sections.title: Why Keep One Archive
sections.content:
The IAB believes the community benefited from a single archival series, where documents are easy to find and retrieve. It says that subseries tend to vanish from the network and that there is no evidence alternate schemes would cause less confusion. Additional documents do not hurt standardization, and the proposed solution is better publicity.

The memo accepts that an informational document can "look like" an official specification, and that vendors might claim conformance to it. The IAB's answer is guidance rather than hiding such documents: there is little evidence of vendors purposely presenting informational or experimental RFCs as Internet standards, and if it happened a proper response would be required.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping every paper on one shelf makes them easy to find. It is better to label the shelf clearly than to hide papers in different rooms.

sections.title: Publication Over Ignorance
sections.content:
The IAB believes the community is best served by openly developed specifications, and that the normal way to develop an Internet protocol specification is through the IETF. It also values access to specifications developed outside the IETF process, because they are experimental, were developed privately, or did not reach the consensus needed for the standards track.

Its position is that publication is better than ignorance: if a specification ends up in products deployed over the Internet, it is better as an easily retrieved RFC than hidden in a private repository. The Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: It is better to share a recipe openly, even if it is not the official one, than to keep it secret.
